prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a discovery in the sense of the prize criteria: a specific idea (trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so the light shift cancels in the clock transition) turned into an instrument that thousands of atoms interrogate at once and that now reaches fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. From the laser-spectroscopy side, what is decisive is that this was not a gradual refinement. It changed the statistical and systematic regime of frequency metrology. It is confirmed by several independent laboratories whose clocks agree with each other, it already supports tests of fundamental constants and of relativistic redshift at the centimetre scale, and it underlies the prospective redefinition of the second. The two-name configuration of Katori (concept and first demonstration) and Ye (accuracy, stability and systematic-control record) is clean and fits the credited list exactly. Of the shortlisted candidates it is the one I can assess most directly, and the evidence for it is the least dependent on interpretation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the prize record for frequency metrology is already dense, with the frequency comb and trapped-ion clock prizes, so some colleagues will see a refinement of an already honoured line of work rather than a new discovery. A second concern is that the opening support is narrow: only Lindroth and I ranked it first, and three other members ranked it fifth or sixth, while several ranked topological insulators and magic-angle graphene far higher. Third, credit among clock groups (PTB, SYRTE, NIST and the Tokyo teams) is wider than two names, and I am working from recollection of who showed what first.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as a clean, concrete advance in precision atomic physics with a clear discovery (magic-wavelength trapping) and a clear instrument, while noting the question of sharing with ion-clock work.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and on the Katori-Ye allocation. On bundling with ion clocks, I would resist it: the ion clock prize rewarded a different physical route (single trapped ions and quantum-logic readout), and merging them would blur the citation and add contestable names beyond the credited list. The lattice clock stands on its own concept, and the citation should say so.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for the combination of a flat-band prediction and the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity, and ranks the lattice clock only sixth because of overlap with prior frequency-metrology prizes.
responses.response: I take the twisted-graphene point seriously, and I do not discount its originality. But maturity is where I differ: the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, the experiments are less than a decade old, and Eriksson himself lists the missing Andrei attribution as a real problem. On the clock overlap, I disagree that the earlier prizes cover it. The comb gave the means to count optical cycles and the ion clock gave a quantum-logic route, but neither contains the magic-wavelength idea or the many-atom lattice regime, which is what produces the 1e-18 stability.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and topological insulators second, as conceptually clean cases where theory predicted and experiment confirmed, and treats the prediction-plus-discovery pairing as the cleaner configuration.
responses.response: Prediction followed by confirmation is indeed the cleanest story, and the clock has it too: the magic-wavelength proposal came first and the strontium demonstration followed. Where I qualify Mehlig is on the topological-insulator side, where he himself notes that the key theory credit (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang) lies outside the supplied names and that the 2D and 3D parts are distinct. That makes a three-person topological prize more contestable on attribution than the clock, and I would put attribution cleanliness above how many members ranked it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first, as a new class of quantum matter with a clean HgTe realisation, and stresses it is a discovery rather than a lifetime body of work.
responses.response: I accept that topological insulators carry the broadest support and are probably the main rival. I would, however, ask whether the committee can defend a three-name set when Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the 2016 prize overlap all enter the discussion. If the committee does choose topological insulators, I would want the citation to be specific about the quantum spin Hall edge states, so as to keep it distinct from the 2016 prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the frequency-metrology line honoured by earlier prizes.
My recollection of the exact priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first demonstrations by other groups is from memory and not verified against the record.

Whether the strongly supported topological-insulator and twisted-graphene candidates can be given clean three-person attributions, which would decide how much weight their wider opening support deserves.
Whether other clock groups (for example PTB and SYRTE teams) deserve credit that a two-name prize would omit.
statement.conflict_note: Possible but indirect: I spent time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is from the JILA frequency-metrology environment around Hall, so I flag that connection. I also work on laser stabilisation and spectral-hole-burning materials, which are technically adjacent to ultra-stable cavity lasers used in the clocks. I have no documented collaboration or institutional tie to Katori or Ye, and no other specific conflict is apparent from my profile.
